title: Job 3:11–19
context: Job is still the speaker. Having cursed the day, he now asks why he did not die at birth (3:11–12) and imagines the rest he would have had among the dead (3:13–19). The grave is pictured as a place of quiet where kings and princes lie alongside infants who never saw light, where the wicked stop troubling, the weary rest, prisoners no longer hear the taskmaster, and the servant is free from his master. These lines are a sufferer’s picture of relief from present pain, not a developed teaching on the afterlife; Job will later speak of Sheol and hope in other ways (14:13–15; 19:25–27). The phrase “built up waste places for themselves” (3:14) is read variously: as rebuilding ruins, or, by some, as monuments or tombs, and the reference is uncertain. Arminian and Reformed readers alike hear this as lament that longs for rest, not as a plan of self-harm, and both look to the rest of Scripture for a fuller word on death and hope.

verses.text: “Why didn’t I die from the womb? Why didn’t I give up the spirit when my mother bore me?
verses.arminianNotes: Job asks why he did not die at birth. Arminian readers hear a genuine question addressed into God’s world, the kind of question Scripture allows in lament (compare Psalm 22:1; Psalm 88), and stress that God does not rebuke Job for asking it in the way the friends later will.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also see a lament of the kind the Psalms record, from a believer who cannot yet see God’s purpose in his life. They hold that the question, though unanswered here, is asked within God’s care. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as grief that longs for relief, not a reasoned rejection of life’s worth.

verses.text: Why did the knees receive me? Or why the breast, that I should nurse?
verses.arminianNotes: Job asks why knees received him and breasts nursed him, the first gestures of care given to an infant. Arminian readers note how suffering can turn even memories of nurture into pain, and they stress that the gift of life Job received was still real even when he cannot feel it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in these first acts of care the providence that kept Job from birth (compare Psalm 22:9–10), which Job now laments without denying. Shared ground: both traditions read the question as the cry of a sufferer, and both hold that the care he received in infancy was God’s gift, not a mistake.

verses.text: For now I should have lain down and been quiet. I should have slept, then I would have been at rest,
verses.arminianNotes: Job imagines that had he died, he would now lie quiet, asleep, and at rest. Arminian readers hear a longing for rest from unrelenting pain, and note that Job speaks of death as sleep and quiet rather than planning to end his life; his longing is for relief that only God can give.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Job’s picture of death as rest is partial, a sufferer’s comparison with his present torment, not a full teaching on the grave. Later Scripture says more about hope beyond death. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse pastorally, as lament, and neither treats it as Job’s settled doctrine of death.

verses.text: with kings and counselors of the earth, who built up waste places for themselves;
verses.arminianNotes: Job pictures himself at rest with kings and counselors who built up waste places for themselves. The phrase may mean rebuilding ruins or, as some suggest, monuments or tombs; it is uncertain. Arminian readers hear Job noting that even great builders end in the same quiet he now longs for.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same leveling of human greatness, which Scripture elsewhere uses to humble pride (compare Psalm 49:10–12; Ecclesiastes 2:16). They hold the image as a sufferer’s comparison, not a theology of the dead. Shared ground: both traditions hedge the phrase and read the point as the equalizing quiet of death.

verses.text: or with princes who had gold, who filled their houses with silver;
verses.arminianNotes: Job adds princes who had gold and filled their houses with silver. Arminian readers note that Job, once among the wealthiest men of the east (1:3), now sees riches as unable to secure anything lasting, and that his longing for rest exposes how little wealth can comfort grief.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same theme: wealth ends at the grave, and the true security of God’s people lies in him, not in gold (compare Psalm 49:16–17). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of Job’s picture of death’s leveling, and both caution against reading it as contempt for the life God gave him.

verses.text: or as a hidden untimely birth I had not been, as infants who never saw light.
verses.arminianNotes: Job wishes he had been like a hidden untimely birth, like infants who never saw light (compare Ecclesiastes 6:3–5). Arminian readers handle this line gently, noting that Job is voicing the depth of his pain, not making a statement about the worth of infants who die, whom God holds in his care.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also treat the line pastorally, as Job’s comparison of his suffering with those who never saw it. They do not use the verse to settle questions about infant death, which Scripture addresses elsewhere. Shared ground: both traditions read it as lament and handle it with care for grieving readers.

verses.text: There the wicked cease from troubling. There the weary are at rest.
verses.arminianNotes: Job describes the grave as where the wicked cease from troubling and the weary are at rest. Arminian readers hear the longing of an exhausted man for rest from trouble, and note that his longing is for a rest he cannot yet see.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in Job’s words a true longing for rest that God answers more fully than Job here imagines. They note that Job speaks of the grave’s quiet, not judgment, because he is lamenting, not teaching. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as lament, not a complete doctrine of death.

verses.text: There the prisoners are at ease together. They don’t hear the voice of the taskmaster.
verses.arminianNotes: Job pictures prisoners at ease together, no longer hearing the taskmaster. Arminian readers note that Job’s suffering makes him identify with the oppressed, and they hear in his words a concern that the God of Scripture shares for those under cruel burdens.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same identification and note that God, who hears the groaning of the oppressed, is the one who finally brings freedom. Job’s picture of the grave is a sufferer’s image of release. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as lament that longs for relief, not as a teaching about the dead.

verses.text: The small and the great are there. The servant is free from his master.
verses.arminianNotes: Job closes this section: small and great are together, and the servant is free from his master. Arminian readers hear death’s equalizing power and Job’s longing to be free of his burden, and note that his words express exhaustion rather than any wish to harm himself.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also see death’s leveling of rank and note that Scripture elsewhere sets this beside the hope of resurrection and judgment. Job’s words are lament, not final doctrine. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of Job’s longing for rest, held within the book’s larger movement toward God’s answer.
